summary.text: At \(n=1\), the sole \(k=0\) summand has \(\beta(0)=t(0)=1\), so \(a(1)=8/2=4\) is even. But \(1=2^0\) is a positive power of two, directly contradicting the asserted parity equivalence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\beta(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{2}\binom{k+j}{j}
\]
be the Apéry number appearing in the definition, and let
\[
t(k)=[x^k](x^2+4x-1)^k
\]
be the indicated generalized central trinomial number. The sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(15k+8)\beta(k)t(k)
\qquad(n>0).
\]
The conjecture asserts, in particular, that for every positive integer \(n\), the integer \(a(n)\) is odd if and only if \(n\) is a power of two.

We disprove the parity assertion by taking \(n=1\).

First compute the two ingredients at \(k=0\). The defining sum for \(\beta(0)\) has only the term \(j=0\), so
\[
\beta(0)=\binom00^2\binom00=1.
\]
Also,
\[
(x^2+4x-1)^0=1,
\]
and hence the coefficient of \(x^0\) is
\[
t(0)=[x^0]1=1.
\]

For \(n=1\), the sum defining \(a(n)\) ranges from \(k=0\) to \(k=n-1=0\), so it consists of exactly one term. Substituting the values just found gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(1)
&=\frac1{2\cdot1}(-1)^0(15\cdot0+8)\beta(0)t(0)\\
&=\frac12\cdot1\cdot8\cdot1\cdot1\\
&=4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a(1)\) is indeed an integer, but it is even: explicitly, \(a(1)=4=2\cdot2\), so it cannot be odd.

On the other hand, \(1\) is a positive power of two, since
\[
1=2^0.
\]
Consequently, at the positive index \(n=1\), the right-hand side of the claimed equivalence—“\(n\) is a power of two”—is true, while the left-hand side—“\(a(n)\) is odd”—is false. Therefore the asserted equivalence fails at \(n=1\), and hence the universal conjecture is false.
